power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

))

# display table -----------------------------------

text.text: Introduction: Understanding suicide risk among men requires attention to psychosocial experiences alongside the gendered expectations shaping their lives.
This study examined associations between demographic, behavioural and psychosocial factors, conformity to masculine norms and suicide risk among men attending an Irish university.

A cross-sectional survey of 512 male university students assessed suicide risk using the Suicide Behaviours Questionnaire-Revised (SBQ-R), alongside demographic characteristics, health behaviours, psychosocial measures and Conformity to Masculine Norms Inventory (CMNI) subscales.

Hierarchical binary logistic regression examined associations with scoring at or above the SBQ-R screening threshold (≥7), entering demographic and behavioural characteristics, psychosocial factors and masculine norms sequentially.
Results: Results: Of 473 participants with available SBQ-R data, 42.5% scored at or above the screening threshold; 64.5% of those with loneliness data met the loneliness criterion.

Participants at or above the SBQ-R threshold reported greater emotional control, violence, playboy and self-reliance norms, lower endorsement of status and work-related norms, and less favourable help-seeking attitudes and intentions.

In the fully adjusted model, higher loneliness (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.24, 95% CI 1.03-1.48) and hopelessness (aOR 1.23, 95% CI 1.04-1.45) were associated with higher odds of scoring at or above the threshold, while greater resilience was associated with lower odds (aOR 0.50, This is a provisional file, not the final typeset article 95% CI 0.33-0.75).

Heterosexual identification was associated with lower odds than non-heterosexual identification (aOR 0.44, 95% CI 0.21-0.93), while drug use was associated with higher odds than no use (aOR 2.00, 95% CI 1.08-3.71).
Psychosocial factors significantly improved model fit (p < .001); masculine norm subscales did not (p = .780).
text.formatted: Psychosocial factors significantly improved model fit (p < .001); masculine norm subscales did not (p = .780).

text.text: Discussion: The findings highlight relational experiences, future expectations and coping resources alongside inequalities among men as relevant to suicide prevention interventions in the university setting.
The limited additional contribution of masculine norm measures warrants distinguishing individual conformity scores from broader gendered experiences.

Gender-responsive prevention should connect accessible individual support with institutional conditions that enable meaningful connection, sustain hope and accommodate diverse identities and circumstances.
Suicide is a major public health concern and the third leading cause of death among people aged 15-29 years globally (World Health, 2026).
text.formatted: Suicide is a major public health concern and the third leading cause of death among people aged 15-29 years globally <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(World Health, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In Ireland, recent data from the Central Statistics Office reported 481 deaths by suicide occurring in 2024, of which 387 (80.5%) were among males (Central Statistics Office, 2026) .

text.text: In addition, as outlined the Movember Institute's 'Real Face of Men's Health Republic of Ireland report, among males aged 15-34 years, external causes of injury, including suicide, account for more than half of all premature deaths, highlighting the disproportionate burden of suicide among younger men (Movember Institute, 2025).
The consequences of such extend beyond those lives lost, affecting the mental health and wellbeing of bereaved families, friends and communities (Cerel et al., 2019; Pitman et al., 2014).

text.text: Understanding the disproportionate burden of suicide mortality among males requires attention to the social conditions and gendered experiences that shape vulnerability and access to support among men and boys (WHO, 2018).

text.text: A social determinants perspective situates suicide within the wider economic, social and environmental conditions of people's lives (Pirkis et al., 2017).

text.text: Evidence linking unemployment, low income and relationship breakdown with higher suicide mortality among men reinforces the importance of considering material circumstances and relational disruption alongside individual psychological factors (Hughes et al., 2025).

text.text: A complementary gendered lens considers how masculine norms and expectations shape men's experiences of distress, relationships and engagement with support, while recognizing differences among men across social circumstances and contexts (Nordin et al., 2024; Seidler et al., 2016; WHO, 2018).

text.text: These perspectives provide a basis for examining suicide risk among men in relation to both their psychosocial experiences and the settings in which they live, study and seek support.
Universities provide an important setting in which to examine these social and gendered influences on mental health.
For many students, entering university coincides with emerging adulthood, a period of identity exploration and changing roles and relationships (Arnett, 2000).
text.formatted: For many students, entering university coincides with emerging adulthood, a period of identity exploration and changing roles and relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Arnett, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: The transition can involve increased academic demands, financial pressures and the challenge of establishing social connections, sometimes away from familiar support networks (Worsley et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The transition can involve increased academic demands, financial pressures and the challenge of establishing social connections, sometimes away from familiar support networks <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Worsley et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: However, students span different ages and life stages, making it important to consider diverse circumstances and experiences of university life.

Research highlights how teaching environments, accommodation and relationships with staff and peers are key considerations in shaping students' experiences of connection and support (Worsley et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Research highlights how teaching environments, accommodation and relationships with staff and peers are key considerations in shaping students' experiences of connection and support <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Worsley et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Within Irish higher education, university belonging and social connectedness are associated with better mental wellbeing, highlighting the importance of opportunities for connection in students' everyday university experiences (McGrath et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Within Irish higher education, university belonging and social connectedness are associated with better mental wellbeing, highlighting the importance of opportunities for connection in students' everyday university experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(McGrath et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These findings support attention to the social and organizational conditions that enable connection, participation and belonging within higher education (McGrath et al., 2026; WHO, 2015).
text.formatted: These findings support attention to the social and organizational conditions that enable connection, participation and belonging within higher education <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(McGrath et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">WHO, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: For men attending university, this provides a rationale for examining psychosocial experiences alongside masculine norms, within an institutional setting that offers opportunities for both prevention and support.
Understanding these experiences within university settings requires attention to the social circumstances students encounter and the psychological resources available to them.

Financial strain and stressful life events, including relationship breakdown, family conflict and employment difficulties, have been associated with suicidal thoughts and behaviors (Currier et al., 2016; Pirkis et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Financial strain and stressful life events, including relationship breakdown, family conflict and employment difficulties, have been associated with suicidal thoughts and behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Currier et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Pirkis et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Relational experiences are also relevant where loneliness is associated with subsequent suicidal ideation and behavior (McClelland et al., 2020), while lower interpersonal trust has been associated with subsequent suicidal ideation in population-based research (Kim et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Relational experiences are also relevant where loneliness is associated with subsequent suicidal ideation and behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(McClelland et al., 2020)</ref>, while lower interpersonal trust has been associated with subsequent suicidal ideation in population-based research <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Kim et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: For boys and young men, the availability of family, friends or other potential sources of support does not necessarily mean that disclosing distress feels safe.
Trust, familiarity and expectations about how others will respond influence informal help-seeking, alongside concerns about stigma and burdening others (Burke et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Trust, familiarity and expectations about how others will respond influence informal help-seeking, alongside concerns about stigma and burdening others <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Burke et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Recent research with men further highlights how anticipated judgement and uncertainty about acceptable emotional disclosure can constrain access to peer support, even where peers are willing to help (Sharp et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Recent research with men further highlights how anticipated judgement and uncertainty about acceptable emotional disclosure can constrain access to peer support, even where peers are willing to help <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Sharp et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In addition accessibility, anonymity, affordability and responsiveness to men's circumstances are cited as important considerations for strengthening trust in This is a provisional file, not the final typeset article services (Movember Institute, 2025).

These relational and institutional conditions provide a context for considering hopelessness and resilience: negative expectations about the future are associated with suicidal ideation and behavior (David Klonsky et al., 2012; Gómez-Tabares et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2020; O'Connor & Nock, 2014; Smith et al., 2008; Tsujii et al., 2020). while a greater perceived capacity to recover from stress has been associated with lower suicidal ideation (Kim et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2008).
text.formatted: These relational and institutional conditions provide a context for considering hopelessness and resilience: negative expectations about the future are associated with suicidal ideation and behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(David Klonsky et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Gómez-Tabares et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Kim et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">O'Connor & Nock, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Smith et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Tsujii et al., 2020)</ref>. while a greater perceived capacity to recover from stress has been associated with lower suicidal ideation <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Kim et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Smith et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Examining these factors together enables consideration of men's social circumstances and psychological experiences without locating responsibility for managing adversity solely within individuals.
Indeed, these social and psychological experiences can also be gendered, with masculine norms shaping expectations about emotional expression, relationships and responses to distress.

Masculinities are socially situated and negotiated through relationships and institutions, meaning that the expectations men encounter, and the consequences of conforming to or departing from them, vary across contexts (Galdas, 2026).
text.formatted: Masculinities are socially situated and negotiated through relationships and institutions, meaning that the expectations men encounter, and the consequences of conforming to or departing from them, vary across contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Galdas, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Norms emphasizing self-reliance and emotional control may constrain disclosure and access to support where vulnerability carries a perceived social cost, while relationships that legitimize openness and mutual care can create opportunities for support (Galdas, 2026; McGrath et al., 2022; Sharp et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Norms emphasizing self-reliance and emotional control may constrain disclosure and access to support where vulnerability carries a perceived social cost, while relationships that legitimize openness and mutual care can create opportunities for support <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Galdas, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">McGrath et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Sharp et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Associations with suicide-related outcomes also differ across particular norms and how they are measured, cautioning against treating masculinity as a uniform risk factor (Starkey & Moore, 2026).
text.formatted: Associations with suicide-related outcomes also differ across particular norms and how they are measured, cautioning against treating masculinity as a uniform risk factor <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Starkey & Moore, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Longitudinal evidence further suggests that particular masculine norms may relate to suicidal ideation through specific psychosocial experiences.

Greater conformity to selfreliance predicted subsequent perceived burdensomeness, which in turn predicted suicidal ideation, whereas corresponding pathways involving thwarted belongingness were not supported (Gagliano et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Greater conformity to selfreliance predicted subsequent perceived burdensomeness, which in turn predicted suicidal ideation, whereas corresponding pathways involving thwarted belongingness were not supported <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Gagliano et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These findings strengthen the rationale for examining masculine norms alongside psychosocial factors while recognising that relationships may differ across norms and interpersonal experiences.
Men's experiences of these norms are further shaped by age, socioeconomic circumstances, ethnicity and sexual orientation.

For sexual minority men, attention to stigma, exclusion and expectations of heterosexual masculinity is therefore important, rather than interpreting sexual orientation itself as an inherent source of vulnerability (Fernandez et al., 2026; Galdas, 2026).
text.formatted: For sexual minority men, attention to stigma, exclusion and expectations of heterosexual masculinity is therefore important, rather than interpreting sexual orientation itself as an inherent source of vulnerability <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Fernandez et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Galdas, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Contemporary measurement research also highlights that individual conformity scores capture particular dimensions of masculine norms and may inadequately represent their relational and cultural contexts (Fisher et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Contemporary measurement research also highlights that individual conformity scores capture particular dimensions of masculine norms and may inadequately represent their relational and cultural contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Fisher et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: University settings bring these questions into focus because students negotiate relationships, identities and expectations of achievement and independence within shared educational and social environments.

Peer relationships and institutional practices provide contexts in which gendered expectations may be reinforced, challenged or accommodated, while universities offer opportunities to connect individual support with everyday conditions that enable belonging and participation (Galdas, 2026; McGrath et al., 2026; Newton et al., 2016).

text.text: Examining masculine norms alongside psychosocial factors within this setting can therefore inform gender-responsive prevention, while recognising that individual measures capture only part of these wider processes.
An important question for prevention is whether specific masculine norms are associated with elevated suicide risk when considered alongside men's psychosocial experiences and social circumstances.

Earlier analysis of the survey underpinning this study identified associations between psychosocial factors, conformity to particular masculine norms, and suicide literacy, stigma and help-seeking attitudes among men at a university in Ireland ( O'Donnell et al., 2025).

text.text: These findings highlighted the relevance of men's social and gendered experiences to their understanding of suicide and attitudes towards seeking support.

They also provided a rationale for examining whether psychosocial factors and masculine norms were associated with elevated suicide risk itself, extending the focus from knowledge and attitudes to suicide-related thoughts and behaviors.
The present analysis extends this work by focusing on elevated suicide risk and examining associations across sociodemographic, behavioral, psychosocial and masculinity-related domains.

Considering these domains together may help identify priorities for gender-responsive prevention, while recognizing that individual-level measures capture only part of the wider social and institutional contexts shaping men's health.

This study therefore aimed to examine associations between sociodemographic characteristics, behavioral factors, psychosocial factors and conformity to masculine norms and elevated suicide risk among men at a university in Ireland.
This study used data from an anonymous cross-sectional online survey of men attending a multicampus technological university in Ireland.
The wider survey examined mental health, suicide-related experiences, suicide literacy, stigma, help-seeking and conformity to masculine norms.
An earlier publication reported analyses of suicide literacy, stigma and help-seeking attitudes (O'Donnell et al., 2025).

text.text: The present study examined sociodemographic, behavioral, psychosocial and masculinityrelated factors associated with elevated suicide risk.
This is a provisional file, not the final typeset article Students were eligible if they identified as a man, were aged 18 years or older, and were enrolled fulltime at the university.
Approximately 9,000 students were recorded as male in university enrolment figures at the time of the study.
These administrative figures provided an approximate recruitment population rather than an exact count of students meeting the study's gender-based eligibility criteria.
Recruitment took place in November 2023 and coincided with campus activities marking International Men's Day.
Invitations containing study information and a link to the Qualtrics survey were circulated through university email.
Additional recruitment included posters with QR codes in communal spaces and promotion at campus health promotion stands.
Students could access and complete the survey online at a time convenient to them.
Participation was voluntary, and 512 students participated.
Recruitment across campuses and academic departments sought to broaden participation, although the resulting sample was self-selected.
Ethical approval was granted by the South East Technological University Carlow Ethics Committee (reference 380).
Participants received study information and provided electronic informed consent before accessing the questionnaire.
All participants were provided with information about university and community mental health support services on completing the survey.
Participants who indicated suicidal thoughts or behaviors were also shown targeted messages directing them to appropriate support services.
A range of instruments outlined in Table 1 were used to capture sociodemographic characteristics, behavioral, psychosocial and suicide-related variables.

text.text: [INSERT Table 1: Summary of Measures Captured in the Survey HERE] 2.5 Statistical analysis Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics, version 31.
Participant characteristics and study measures were summarized using frequencies and percentages for categorical variables and means and standard deviations for continuous variables.
Available observations were used for descriptive analyses, with denominators reported where missing data resulted in variation in sample size.

Suicide risk was examined using both continuous SBQ-R scores and screening status, dichotomised as below the screening threshold (<7) or at or above the screening threshold for elevated suicide risk (≥7).
text.formatted: Suicide risk was examined using both continuous SBQ-R scores and screening status, dichotomised as below the screening threshold (<7) or at or above the screening threshold for elevated suicide risk (≥7).

text.text: Independent-samples t-tests compared mean SBQ-R scores between two-group categories, while oneway analysis of variance examined differences across categories with more than two groups.
Bonferroni-adjusted post-hoc comparisons were used to examine pairwise differences where reported.
Pearson correlations assessed associations between continuous SBQ-R scores and continuous study measures.

Independent-samples t-tests also compared psychosocial measures, masculine norm subscales, suicide-related attitudes, suicide literacy and help-seeking measures between the two SBQ-R screening groups.
Welch's t-tests were used for comparisons where equal variances were not assumed.
Hierarchical binary logistic regression examined adjusted associations with scoring at or above the SBQ-R screening threshold.

Explanatory variables were entered in four conceptual blocks: Complete-case analysis was used for the regression, with the same participants included across all four blocks to allow model comparisons.
Adjusted odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals were reported.
Changes in model fit following the addition of each block were assessed using likelihood-ratio chisquare tests.
Nagelkerke's pseudo-R² was reported as a descriptive index of model fit.
The Hosmer-Lemeshow test assessed goodness of fit, and classification performance within the analysis sample was summarised using a predicted probability cut-off of .50.
Multicollinearity was examined using variance inflation factors and tolerance statistics.
All statistical tests were two-sided, with statistical significance set at p < .05.

text.text: Among participants with available age data (n = 362), the mean age was 21.84 years (SD 6.09; range 18-69).

In relation to health behaviours, 15.4% met the study's screening criterion for harmful alcohol consumption, while 38.2% reported regular illicit drug use.

Among respondents to the mental health items, 80.4% reported symptoms of, or treatment for, at least one mental health difficulty during the previous 12 months, most commonly anxiety (51.9%) and depression (39.4%).

Additionally, 58.7% reported at least one serious life event during the previous 12 months.

This study examined psychosocial factors and masculine norms associated with suicide risk among men at a university in Ireland.
Among participants with available SBQ-R data, 42.5% scored at or above the screening threshold for elevated suicide risk.
In the fully adjusted model, greater loneliness and hopelessness were associated with higher odds of scoring at or above this threshold, whereas greater resilience was associated with lower odds.
Differences were also observed by heterosexual identification and drug-use status.
Adding psychosocial factors substantially improved model fit beyond demographic and behavioural characteristics.

Although several masculine norm subscales differed between participants below and at or above the threshold in unadjusted analyses, their addition did not significantly improve the multivariable model.
These findings highlight the need to consider men's social experiences and psychological resources alongside gendered norms when examining suicide risk in university settings.

They do not establish the direction of these relationships or imply that masculine norms are unimportant but highlight that the selected subscales did not demonstrate additional statistical contributions after adjustment for the other measured factors.
The association between loneliness and elevated suicide risk places the experience of connection at the center of understanding men's mental health within university settings.

This finding is consistent with prospective evidence linking loneliness with suicidal ideation and behavior, and with theoretical accounts emphasizing the significance of belonging to suicidal distress (McClelland et al., 2020; Van Orden et al., 2010).
text.formatted: This finding is consistent with prospective evidence linking loneliness with suicidal ideation and behavior, and with theoretical accounts emphasizing the significance of belonging to suicidal distress <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(McClelland et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Van Orden et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Connection, however, involves more than the presence of social contacts.

Emotional and social loneliness represent distinguishable experiences among university students, highlighting why participation in a peer network may coexist with an absence of close, dependable support (Diehl et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Emotional and social loneliness represent distinguishable experiences among university students, highlighting why participation in a peer network may coexist with an absence of close, dependable support <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Diehl et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: A gendered interpretation asks whether men can express uncertainty, acknowledge difficulty and seek care without anticipating a loss of acceptance or standing.

Masculine expectations concerning emotional control and self-reliance can influence these negotiations, while distress may remain concealed within efforts to maintain an acceptable social identity (Cleary, 2012; Nordin et al., 2024; Seidler et al., 2016; Seidler et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Masculine expectations concerning emotional control and self-reliance can influence these negotiations, while distress may remain concealed within efforts to maintain an acceptable social identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Cleary, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Nordin et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Seidler et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Seidler et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: These dynamics also have implications for structural and systems-level change.
Universities shape opportunities for connection through teaching arrangements, campus spaces, student participation and access to support.

Addressing loneliness therefore requires coordinated action across academic, administrative and support functions to reduce barriers to participation and create environments in which vulnerability is met with recognition and care.

This includes examining whose circumstances are accommodated by existing arrangements, particularly students whose commuting, employment or financial pressures limit their opportunities to develop dependable relationships (McGrath et al., 2026; Newton et al., 2016).
text.formatted: This includes examining whose circumstances are accommodated by existing arrangements, particularly students whose commuting, employment or financial pressures limit their opportunities to develop dependable relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(McGrath et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Newton et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This interpretation also moves beyond the framing of men as inherently reluctant or unable to connect (Sharp et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This interpretation also moves beyond the framing of men as inherently reluctant or unable to connect <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Sharp et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Shared activity, practical assistance and informal interaction can provide meaningful opportunities for care, reciprocity and health engagement (McGrath et al., 2022; Oliffe et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Shared activity, practical assistance and informal interaction can provide meaningful opportunities for care, reciprocity and health engagement <ref type="bibr">(McGrath et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Oliffe et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Gender-transformative work within community settings illustrates how approaches grounded in familiar social settings can build on these resources while broadening opportunities for support and participation (McGrath et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Gender-transformative work within community settings illustrates how approaches grounded in familiar social settings can build on these resources while broadening opportunities for support and participation <ref type="bibr">(McGrath et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The issue is therefore whether men's relationships accommodate vulnerability and changing needs rather than conforming to a particular model of emotional intimacy.

Research concerning mental health within and after men's intimate partnerships similarly draws attention to relationship dynamics, rather than relationship status alone, in understanding access to support (Oliffe et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Research concerning mental health within and after men's intimate partnerships similarly draws attention to relationship dynamics, rather than relationship status alone, in understanding access to support <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Oliffe et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These perspectives position the quality, flexibility and perceived safety of relationships as central questions for gender-responsive prevention.
Within higher education, these relational processes intersect with belonging and sense of place.

Recent Irish evidence associates university belonging and social connectedness with better mental wellbeing, reinforcing the importance of environments in which students feel recognized, valued and able to participate meaningfully (McGrath et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Recent Irish evidence associates university belonging and social connectedness with better mental wellbeing, reinforcing the importance of environments in which students feel recognized, valued and able to participate meaningfully <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(McGrath et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The transition into university involves renegotiating relationships and support alongside new academic and personal expectations (Worsley et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The transition into university involves renegotiating relationships and support alongside new academic and personal expectations <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Worsley et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: For younger men, this also involves navigating expectations of independence, success and emotional openness, informed by experiences carried forward from boyhood and earlier social settings (Rice et al., 2021; Rice et al., 2018).
text.formatted: For younger men, this also involves navigating expectations of independence, success and emotional openness, informed by experiences carried forward from boyhood and earlier social settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Rice et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Rice et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: These expectations may be contradictory where encouragement to communicate vulnerability can coexist with enduring expectations of self-sufficiency, economic provision and achievement.
Breadwinner identities for instance, may remain culturally influential even where secure employment, affordable housing and financial independence are difficult to attain (Syrda, 2020).
text.formatted: Breadwinner identities for instance, may remain culturally influential even where secure employment, affordable housing and financial independence are difficult to attain <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Syrda, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This can create intergenerational tensions around what becoming an adult man should involve, particularly when inherited markers of success are poorly aligned with contemporary opportunities to achieve them (Hughes et al., 2025; Mokhwelepa & Sumbane, 2025).
text.formatted: This can create intergenerational tensions around what becoming an adult man should involve, particularly when inherited markers of success are poorly aligned with contemporary opportunities to achieve them <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Hughes et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Mokhwelepa & Sumbane, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, uncertainty about identity and the future is situated within a potential mismatch between gendered expectations and the material conditions through which they can be realized.
These conditions also shape opportunities for connection during university life.

Financial pressures, paid employment and commuting can constrain the time and flexibility available to develop relationships, particularly where belonging depends on sustained participation beyond scheduled teaching (McGrath et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Financial pressures, paid employment and commuting can constrain the time and flexibility available to develop relationships, particularly where belonging depends on sustained participation beyond scheduled teaching <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(McGrath et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Changing expectations of masculinity may open possibilities for more supportive relationships, but these possibilities require environments in which vulnerability is accepted and participation is This is a provisional file, not the final typeset article practically attainable.
The potential for vulnerability to deepen connection depends partly on how others respond and whether that response is experienced as understanding, validating and caring.
Earlier experiences of ridicule, dismissal or support may shape both men's willingness to disclose difficulty and their expectations of how disclosure will be received (Neilson & Maitland, 2025).
text.formatted: Earlier experiences of ridicule, dismissal or support may shape both men's willingness to disclose difficulty and their expectations of how disclosure will be received <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Neilson & Maitland, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Qualitative evidence also identifies uncertainty about how much distress can be shared within male friendships, alongside experiences of support that fails to meet the needs being expressed [19].
text.formatted: Qualitative evidence also identifies uncertainty about how much distress can be shared within male friendships, alongside experiences of support that fails to meet the needs being expressed <ref type="bibr">[19]</ref>.

text.text: Encouraging disclosure therefore needs to be accompanied by attention to peers' capacity to recognise and respond to vulnerability.

For universities, fostering a sense of place consequently involves addressing both the relational culture of campus life and the material barriers that make connection less accessible to some students (Higher Education Authority, 2021).
These tensions also provide a context for understanding the association between hopelessness and elevated suicide risk.

Hopelessness was associated with elevated suicide risk, consistent with evidence linking negative expectations about the future with suicidal ideation and behaviour (David Klonsky et al., 2012; O'Connor & Nock, 2014; Tsujii et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Hopelessness was associated with elevated suicide risk, consistent with evidence linking negative expectations about the future with suicidal ideation and behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(David Klonsky et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">O'Connor & Nock, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Tsujii et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This finding extends the discussion from present relationships to students' perceptions of what lies ahead.

University is often understood as a pathway towards opportunity and independence, yet this period also involves uncertainty about identity, educational progression and future prospects (Arnett, 2000; Keshoofy et al., 2023).
text.formatted: University is often understood as a pathway towards opportunity and independence, yet this period also involves uncertainty about identity, educational progression and future prospects <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Arnett, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Keshoofy et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Expectations of achievement and self-sufficiency may influence how some men interpret setbacks and whether they feel able to acknowledge difficulty (Cleary, 2012; Rice et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Expectations of achievement and self-sufficiency may influence how some men interpret setbacks and whether they feel able to acknowledge difficulty <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Cleary, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Rice et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond a psychosocial resource, hope is therefore relevant in relation to the social and material conditions through which a viable future becomes imaginable.
A public health response would connect support for distress with practical assistance and accessible pathways through academic, financial and personal difficulties (Higher Education Authority, 2021).
In addition, the inverse association between resilience and elevated suicide risk complements this emphasis on hope and support.

Resilience is recognized as relevant to suicidal ideation and prevention, with perceived capacity to recover from stress offering one dimension of how people respond to adversity (Kim et al., 2020; Sher, 2019; Smith et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Resilience is recognized as relevant to suicidal ideation and prevention, with perceived capacity to recover from stress offering one dimension of how people respond to adversity <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Kim et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Sher, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Smith et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Within men's health promotion, however, resilience should not become an additional expectation to withstand difficulty independently (Galdas, 2026).
text.formatted: Within men's health promotion, however, resilience should not become an additional expectation to withstand difficulty independently <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Galdas, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Such a framing risks reinforcing forms of self-reliance associated with poorer mental healthrelated outcomes and barriers to help-seeking (Galdas, 2026; Wong et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Such a framing risks reinforcing forms of self-reliance associated with poorer mental healthrelated outcomes and barriers to help-seeking <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Galdas, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Wong et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: A gender-responsive approach instead recognizes flexibility, interdependence and accepting assistance as compatible with resilience, while acknowledging that some sources of adversity lie beyond individual control.

This connects work on coping resources with the development of supportive environments, avoiding an exclusive focus on helping students adapt to pressures that institutions may be able to reduce (Abulfaraj et al., 2024; Newton et al., 2016).
text.formatted: This connects work on coping resources with the development of supportive environments, avoiding an exclusive focus on helping students adapt to pressures that institutions may be able to reduce <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abulfaraj et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Newton et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Universities also operate within wider housing, employment and economic conditions that they cannot resolve alone.

Their role nevertheless includes mitigating the effects of these pressures, advocating for structural responses and ensuring that students' difficulty in managing them is not interpreted as a personal failure of resilience.
Indeed, attention to the conditions that support resilience also requires recognizing that exposure to adversity and access to support are unequally distributed among men.

Differences by sexual orientation reinforce this point, with lower adjusted odds of elevated suicide risk among participants identifying as heterosexual broadly consistent with evidence of inequalities in suicidality by sexual orientation (Ramchand et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Differences by sexual orientation reinforce this point, with lower adjusted odds of elevated suicide risk among participants identifying as heterosexual broadly consistent with evidence of inequalities in suicidality by sexual orientation <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Ramchand et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Minority stress theory locates these inequalities within socially produced pressures, including stigma, discrimination and anticipated rejection, rather than treating sexual orientation as an inherent vulnerability (Frost & Meyer, 2023).

text.text: This provides a gendered lens through which to consider whose identities are affirmed and whose belonging may be conditional on conformity to prevailing expectations of masculinity and heterosexuality.
As such, inclusive prevention should extend beyond designated services to everyday experiences of recognition, safety and participation.

The objective is an institutional environment in which men with diverse identities can access support and contribute to university life without concealment or pressure to conform ( O'Donnell et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The objective is an institutional environment in which men with diverse identities can access support and contribute to university life without concealment or pressure to conform ( <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">O'Donnell et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Attention to the conditions of participation also raises questions about how students find connection within peer environments, including those where substance use forms part of social interaction (Stritzel, 2022).
text.formatted: Attention to the conditions of participation also raises questions about how students find connection within peer environments, including those where substance use forms part of social interaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Stritzel, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Drug-use status was also associated with elevated suicide risk, with lower adjusted odds among nonusers than among participants reporting use even below the heavy-use threshold.

This aligns with evidence linking substance use with suicidal thoughts and behaviors and supports integrating substance-use responses within student mental health provision (Giugovaz et al., 2024; Welsh et al., 2019).

text.text: A gendered perspective places these behaviors within the wider contexts of coping, peer affiliation and expectations concerning risk-taking and emotional expression (Rice et al., 2021; WHO, 2018).
text.formatted: A gendered perspective places these behaviors within the wider contexts of coping, peer affiliation and expectations concerning risk-taking and emotional expression <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Rice et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">WHO, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This raises a potential tension where settings that provide social connection also involve exposure to harm.
Prevention approaches should therefore combine accessible, non-judgmental support with varied opportunities for belonging that do not depend on substance use.
The findings concerning masculine norms reinforce the importance of distinguishing particular expectations from masculinity as a whole.
Several subscales differed between the SBQ-R threshold groups in unadjusted analyses, but their addition did not significantly improve the fully adjusted model.
This finding sits alongside evidence of domain-specific relationships between masculine norms, mental health, suicidal ideation and help-seeking (Benakovic et al., 2025; Wong et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This finding sits alongside evidence of domain-specific relationships between masculine norms, mental health, suicidal ideation and help-seeking <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Benakovic et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Wong et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Interpretation also requires attention to how masculinity is operationalized.

The CMNI subscales assess individual conformity to specified norms and do not encompass the full range of masculine identities, practices or relationships which raises a broader conceptual issue of which dimensions of gender are made visible through standardized measures, and which remain outside their scope (Fisher et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The CMNI subscales assess individual conformity to specified norms and do not encompass the full range of masculine identities, practices or relationships which raises a broader conceptual issue of which dimensions of gender are made visible through standardized measures, and which remain outside their scope <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Fisher et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This distinction is consistent with a relational understanding of masculinities as configurations of practice shaped by gender relations, power and historical and social contexts, rather than fixed sets of individual traits (Connell & Messerschmidt, 2005).
text.formatted: This distinction is consistent with a relational understanding of masculinities as configurations of practice shaped by gender relations, power and historical and social contexts, rather than fixed sets of individual traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Connell & Messerschmidt, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Masculine expectations may be reinforced, contested or reworked across relationships and settings, with different consequences for men's opportunities to express distress and access care.

Standardised conformity scores therefore provide useful evidence about particular norms, while offering a partial account of how masculinities are enacted and negotiated across cultural contexts, generations and institutional environments.

A contextual approach considers individual conformity alongside expectations operating within relationships and institutions, including how vulnerability is received and which forms of assistance become acceptable and accessible (Galdas, 2026; Nordin et al., 2024).
text.formatted: A contextual approach considers individual conformity alongside expectations operating within relationships and institutions, including how vulnerability is received and which forms of assistance become acceptable and accessible <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Galdas, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Nordin et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: For university suicide prevention, this directs attention towards responsive individual support and institutional conditions that enable diverse groups of men to experience belonging, sustain hope and obtain assistance.
It brings gender-responsive practice into a settings-based public health approach, addressing students' immediate needs alongside the environments that shape their opportunities for wellbeing.

A strength of this study is its examination of demographic, behavioral, psychosocial and masculine norm variables within a single analytical framework, contributing evidence on suicide risk among men in an Irish university setting.
Several limitations should nevertheless inform interpretation.
The crosssectional design prevents conclusions about temporal order or causality.
Loneliness, hopelessness, resilience and substance use may precede, accompany or follow suicide-related distress.
The findings cannot establish mediation or explain why the masculine norm subscales did not contribute significantly after adjustment.
Similarly, scoring at or above the SBQ-R threshold represents a screening indicator rather than a clinical assessment of current suicide risk.
The proportion exceeding this threshold should not be interpreted as the prevalence of current suicidal intent or the likelihood of subsequent suicide.
Recruitment relied on voluntary participation at a single multi-campus university, creating potential for self-selection bias.
Students experiencing distress or with a particular interest in mental health may have been more likely to participate.
The findings therefore cannot be assumed to represent all men attending the university, students at other institutions or men outside higher education.
Although the sample predominantly comprised younger adults, its wider age range also means that the findings should not be interpreted exclusively as reflecting young men's experiences.
The regression included 305 complete cases from 515 dataset records.
Exclusion of participants with missing model data reduced precision and may have introduced selection bias if those included differed systematically from those excluded.
Self-reported measures may be affected by recall and social desirability, particularly for sensitive experiences and behaviors.
The CMNI subscales capture individual endorsement of particular norms rather than the full range of relational, cultural and institutional processes through which gender operates.
Longitudinal and qualitative research would help clarify how gendered social conditions, relationships and psychological experiences interact over time.
This study sought to examine psychosocial factors and masculine norms associated with suicide risk among men in a university setting.

Understanding these associations through a gendered lens requires attention to how expectations of masculinity interact with the relationships, institutions and material circumstances shaping men's lives.

The conditions under which men feel valued, envisage a viable future and seek support are central to this understanding, alongside the inequalities that make these possibilities less accessible to some men.

Gender-responsive prevention must therefore extend beyond encouraging men to disclose distress or cope more effectively to address how vulnerability is received, how belonging becomes possible and whether meaningful support follows.
Universities have a role in shaping these conditions through everyday relationships, inclusive institutional practices and practical responses to the pressures students face.
This places shared responsibility for connection, care and opportunity at the center of suicide prevention.
